final.title: Shared logins hide a workflow cost you only notice later
final.body:
Shared logins are usually a convenience choice, not a strategy. For an owner-run small business, the hidden cost is not abstract: you lose the clean record of who changed what, who still has access, and who handed the password to the next person. That turns a simple account into a small audit problem.

The workarounds are familiar. Someone keeps a password note, a spreadsheet, or becomes the human router for every account. It keeps things moving, but only just.

The practical next step is simple: ask, “Who has access to our shared accounts, who gave it to them, and when should that access end?” If nobody can answer that cleanly, you have found the gap. Treat that as a workflow decision, not a technology one.

Then do one manual pass: list the shared accounts, note who actually needs each one, and write down the owner for each access grant. Once the access record exists, you can decide whether the right fix is a password manager, role-based access, or leaving it manual for now.

Shared logins work until they don’t. That is usually when the missing record shows up.

final.title: Shared logins hide an access problem, not just a password problem
final.body:
Shared logins are usually a convenience choice, not a strategy. For an owner-operator, the real issue is the access trail: who has the account, who added them, and when their access should end. Once that record is fuzzy, even a small mistake takes longer to untangle.

The usual workaround is familiar: a password note, a spreadsheet, or one person acting as the human router for every account. It keeps work moving, but only just.

Here is the practical diagnostic question: who has access to your shared accounts, who granted it, and when will it be removed? If nobody can answer cleanly, you have found the workflow gap.

The next step is simple. Audit the shared accounts, list who actually needs each one, and document the handoff for adding or removing access. That is a bounded workflow decision, not a tooling puzzle. Shared logins work until they do not.

post.title: Shared logins hide an access problem, not just a password problem
post.body:
Shared logins are usually a convenience choice, not a strategy. In a small business, the quiet cost is not the password itself. It is the missing record of who has access, who granted it, and when it should end. Once that trail disappears, a simple mistake takes longer to untangle, and offboarding gets messy.

The usual workaround is familiar: a password note, a spreadsheet, or one person acting as the human router for every account. It keeps the work moving, but only just.

The practical next step is simple: ask, “Who has access to our shared accounts, who added them, and when will they lose it?” If nobody can answer cleanly, you have found the workflow gap.

That is the point where you decide whether the fix is better access documentation, role-based access, or a more formal password process. Shared logins work until they do not. Small teams usually notice the cost at the least convenient moment.
